easy.heading: Warming Up With Some Simple Matches
easy.body:
Starting today's puzzle felt like a nice breeze. I immediately zoomed in on the bottom left corner where there was a sum target of 2 for cells (5,0) and (5,1). Since we only have two spots to fill, it was a safe bet that both cells needed to be 1. I looked over at my pile of dominoes and saw the [0,1] and [5,1] pieces, which gave me some great starting options. 

Another spot that caught my eye was the equals region at (0,3) and (0,4). This is always a fun constraint because it acts like a mirror. Once I realized that (1,4) had to be less than 5, it really narrowed down which domino could sit in that vertical slot. I ended up placing the [0,1] domino near the top left and everything else just seemed to click into place. It is all about finding those small anchors and building out from there.

medium.heading: Navigating the Middle Ground
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today definitely stepped things up with that huge equals region spanning four different cells. Seeing (0,5), (1,5), (2,4), and (2,5) all tied together meant I had to find a value that repeated across several of my dominoes. I spent a good minute just staring at my [3,3], [4,4], and [1,1] pieces to see which one could bridge that gap. 

The sum of 10 at the top was the real breakthrough for me. To hit 10 with just two cells at (0,3) and (0,4), you really need those high-value pips. Using the [6,4] domino there was a total game changer. It also helped that (3,0) was marked as an empty cell, which functioned like a roadblock, telling me exactly where I couldn't put my larger pieces. Once the top row was settled, the bottom half with the sum of 3 constraints felt much more manageable.

hard.heading: Cracking the Code on a Tough Grid
hard.body:
Wow, the hard puzzle really lived up to its name today! The standout challenge was definitely that sum of 17 across three cells in the bottom row. Math-wise, there are only a few ways to get that high with domino pips, usually involving a combination of 6s and 5s. I held onto my [6,6] and [5,6] pieces like they were gold until I figured out exactly how they needed to sit to satisfy the sum of 17 at (5,1), (5,2), and (5,3). 

I actually hit a bit of a dead end near the center where the equals region at (2,1), (3,1), and (3,2) met the sum of 4. I originally tried to put a 2 in there, but it messed up the nearby greater than 3 constraint at (3,4). The real trick was balancing the low sum of 2 at the top with the high sum at the bottom. It felt like a tug-of-war for the best dominoes! Finally seeing the unequal constraint at the end confirm my last two pieces was such a satisfying moment.

explanation.tips: Always look for the highest and lowest sum constraints first because they have the fewest possible combinations. If you see an empty cell constraint, treat it as a fixed zero or a starting point to eliminate dominoes that do not have a blank side. Also, try to place your doubles early if they fit an equals region, as they are often the key to those tricky mirrored sections.
explanation.learned: Today really highlighted how important the empty cell constraints are for narrowing down your path. I used to ignore them and focus on the sums, but they are actually secret weapons for ruling out high-value dominoes in specific corners. I also noticed that when you have a sum of 17 like we did in the hard puzzle, you are almost always going to be using your 6-6 or 5-6 pieces, so it pays to set those aside early in your planning.

faqs.question: What does the empty constraint mean in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: In the Pips puzzle, an empty constraint typically means the cell must contain zero pips, which corresponds to the blank side of a domino.

faqs.question: How do you solve a sum region in Pips?
faqs.answer: To solve a sum region, you must place dominoes so that the total number of dots in the highlighted cells adds up exactly to the target number shown in the corner.

faqs.question: Can I reuse dominoes in the same puzzle?
faqs.answer: No, each domino provided in the list for a specific puzzle can only be used once. Part of the challenge is managing your inventory as you fill the grid.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy for hard Pips puzzles?
faqs.answer: Start by identifying the most restrictive regions, such as very large sums or very small sums. These limit your domino choices significantly and create a framework for the rest of the board.

faqs.question: Is there a daily NYT Pips hint?
faqs.answer: While the NYT doesn't provide official hints, looking for regions with only one possible mathematical solution is the best way to get yourself un-stuck every day.
